items.title: Targeted checks highlight opportunities to lift safety in joinery sector
items.summary: A recent WorkSafe initiative has found many joinery businesses could benefit from improving how they manage machine safety, workplace health risks, and hazardous substances.
items.readerText:
A recent WorkSafe initiative has found many joinery businesses could benefit from improving how they manage machine safety, workplace health risks, and hazardous substances.

The insights come from proactive visits to more than 600 wood product manufacturing businesses between January and March this year, including over 100 joinery workshops, most of them small to medium-sized.

Manufacturing remains one of Aotearoa New Zealand’s highest harm sectors. It accounts for the highest rate and number of injuries with more than a week off work, with around 200 injuries each year involving machinery.

WorkSafe’s assessments focused on the critical risks most likely to cause serious harm: machine safety, exposure to wood dust, fumes and chemicals, and hazardous substances management.

More than 85 percent of joinery businesses that were assessed by WorkSafe inspectors received guidance and practical support to strengthen their health and safety practices.

Project lead Savio Valladares says the most common areas needing improvement were machine safety, hazardous substances management, and local exhaust ventilation.

However, he emphasises that practical improvements are within reach.

“Making work safer starts with the basics – good training and worker engagement, effective supervision, properly guarded and maintained machinery, and controlling dust and fumes,” he says.

Managing the risks of exposure to wood dust was a consistent issue. Among the businesses assessed, common gaps included poor housekeeping, limited training, and incorrect selection or use of personal protective equipment (PPE). Overall, 56 percent had PPE-related issues.

“Exposure to wood dust can have serious long-term health effects,” says Savio Valladares. “Simple steps like choosing the right respirator and making sure it fits properly can make a big difference.”

Hazardous substances management also stood out, with 60% of businesses needing improvement. In many cases, basic information such as safety data sheets or inventories were missing.

WorkSafe’s Hazardous Substances Principal Advisor Susan Collier says these gaps can leave workers exposed to both immediate and long-term harm.

“The consequences of not properly managing hazardous substances can be immediate – people can be overwhelmed by toxic gases and burned by spills. But what’s more common is that people may be exposed but they don’t feel the effects until many years later.”

She says there are ways of working with these substances that ensure worker safety – and a good starting point is the safety data sheets which businesses can get from their suppliers.

“We also have a Hazardous Substances Calculator available online. And if you input your data it’ll spit out a controls report specific to your business, to help with safe storage and management. It’s really useful and businesses don’t have to navigate this alone.”

That’s a sentiment that’s echoed by Savio Valladares: “Our inspectors have a lot of knowledge and information available, which can help ensure workplaces are safer and better for everyone.”

“Another thing that can really help is looking inside your business – good worker engagement can help identify and address some of these problems. It really is at the heart of what we do and can be a really valuable tool for businesses.”

Businesses can find guidance on managing manufacturing risks on the WorkSafe website.

From shutdown to turnaround – an example of WorkSafe intervention

When WorkSafe inspector Mike McConnell arrived at a small joinery business for a routine visit, the situation was serious.

Dust coated almost every surface. Offcuts surrounded machinery, creating trip and fire risks. Dust extraction units were running but not connected.

“They were just sucking air,” he says. “Electrical risks were visible. A worker was operating alone in the workshop, breathing in fine wood dust.

Work couldn’t continue. A prohibition notice, a legal direction that stops work immediately when there’s serious risk of harm, was issued.

For the owner, who asked to remain anonymous, it was confronting but fair. “I knew it had got too bad,” he says. “It needed to be cleaned up.”

What followed was a focused turnaround. With support from WorkSafe, the workshop closed for a week. The space was thoroughly cleaned, extraction systems repaired, electrical risks addressed, and housekeeping rebuilt.

Just as importantly, the focus shifted to worker health. The owner learned more about wood dust risks, arranged health monitoring, and made sure proper personal protective equipment was available. “I didn’t realise how much the evidence had changed over the years,” he says. “You’ve got to take it seriously now.”

The prohibition notice still hangs on the wall as a conversation starter.

“I’ve heard people dismiss WorkSafe and its inspectors in the past, but in my experience, they’ve provided really useful advice – they’re able to look at my workshop with a fresh set of eyes and point out risks that I don’t see.

“WorkSafe are welcome to come into my workshop – their advice could save my, or someone else’s, arm or a leg. Why would you want to avoid that?”

For WorkSafe’s Mike McConnell the visit reinforces what the job is all about: “This was the best result, a huge improvement in health and safety without anyone having to suffer an injury first.

“Everyone worked together to ensure the business got back up and running as quickly as possible. It’s satisfying when we can work closely with others to help them identify and address hazards before someone gets hurt.”

items.title: New guidance released for upcoming HSWA changes
items.summary: WorkSafe has released the first in a series of guidance products to help businesses prepare for upcoming changes to the Health and Safety at Work Act (HSWA).
items.readerText:
WorkSafe has released the first in a series of guidance products to help businesses prepare for upcoming changes to the Health and Safety at Work Act (HSWA).

The new guidance focuses on two concepts that help shape the amendments, namely critical risk and the size of a business or organisation. These concepts will play an important role in determining how the amended legislation applies to different businesses when it comes into force on 1 April 2027.

The guidance outlines the difference between critical risk and other risk, how businesses can determine whether they are considered small or large under the Act, and the duties that apply to each. The guidance is now available on the WorkSafe website:

Prioritising critical risks for large PCBUs

This is the first step in a broader programme of support for businesses. Over the coming months WorkSafe will continue releasing guidance, tools and educational resources to help businesses build their understanding of the amendments and prepare for the changes ahead.

items.title: Manufacturing businesses invest $490k into hazardous substances safety following worker harm
items.summary: This year, two manufacturing businesses have completed enforceable undertakings with WorkSafe New Zealand, following separate incidents where workers were harmed by hazardous substances.
items.readerText:
This year, two manufacturing businesses have completed enforceable undertakings with WorkSafe New Zealand, following separate incidents where workers were harmed by hazardous substances.

An enforceable undertaking (EU) is a legally binding agreement that serves as an alternative to prosecution.

Under an EU, a business accepts responsibility for a health and safety failure and commits to improving health and safety practices in its workplace. The business must also share lessons learned with the wider industry and make amends to victims, either through financial compensation or other agreed forms of remediation.

These EUs highlight the importance of managing one of manufacturing's most significant health and safety risks.

The first, involving the meat processor Silver Fern Farms, follows a 2022 incident where two workers were hospitalised after inhaling a hazardous substance while cleaning the company's Hokitika plant.

WorkSafe’s investigation found the company failed to ensure worker safety while a cleaning chemical was being used.

Silver Fern Farms has now completed more than $170,000 worth of improvements, including safer chemical dispensing systems, hazardous substances training, stronger chemical first-aid arrangements, personal protective equipment (PPE) improvements, and an industry-wide programme to share lessons learned. It also paid reparations to the victims.

The EU for the cleaning products manufacturer Ecostore follows a 2023 incident in which a worker suffered permanent eye injuries after being sprayed with a hazardous liquid when a pressurised hose came loose during dishwasher powder manufacturing.

WorkSafe's investigation found shortcomings in the company’s chemical safety management, including PPE, worker training, and emergency management arrangements.

Ecostore has now completed more than $323,000 in health and safety improvements, including changes to chemical handling processes, stronger PPE controls, additional worker training, and new equipment designed to reduce spills and splash hazards.

The company also provided financial amends to the injured worker and shared its learnings with industry through workshops, case studies and other initiatives.

WorkSafe's Head of Regulatory Services Tracey Conlon says the enforcement reflects the seriousness of the risk.

“Hazardous substances are a significant health and safety risk in manufacturing because exposure to some substances can cause serious injury, illness, or long-term health problems.

“When carrying out inspections at manufacturing businesses our inspectors have seen significant gaps in safe management of hazardous substances, whether that's understanding the risks, ensuring workers have the right training and protective equipment, or knowing how to respond if something goes wrong.”

Tracey Conlon says the actions completed under these EUs demonstrate the value of learning from incidents and sharing those lessons with others.

“Both Silver Fern Farms and Ecostore undertook significant programmes of work to improve how hazardous substances are managed in their workplaces.

“One of the strengths of the EU process is that it creates opportunities for practical lessons to be shared across an entire sector. The aim is not only to address harm at one workplace, but to help prevent similar incidents elsewhere.”

Inadequate hazardous substances management is not unique to manufacturing.

Recent WorkSafe assessments of hundreds of agricultural and horticultural businesses found it was a common issue for those industries too.

items.title: WorkSafe inspectors head to farms and residential builds in proactive safety push
items.summary: WorkSafe New Zealand health and safety inspectors will carry out proactive assessment visits to beef and lamb farms and residential construction sites across Aotearoa New Zealand from October to December 2026.
items.readerText:
WorkSafe New Zealand health and safety inspectors will carry out proactive assessment visits to beef and lamb farms and residential construction sites across Aotearoa New Zealand from October to December 2026.

The visits will focus on how businesses are managing critical health and safety risks – such as vehicles, hazardous substances and remote work on farms, and falls from working at height on residential construction sites.

WorkSafe is focusing on agriculture and construction because of the high numbers of deaths and serious injuries in these sectors.

“These proactive visits to workplaces in high-risk industries help ensure businesses and workers understand their health and safety responsibilities,” says WorkSafe’s Head of Inspectorate Rob Pope.

“It gives our inspectors the opportunity to talk with people on site about how they keep themselves and others safe, and provide guidance to make improvements where needed.”

Information gathered from assessments also gives WorkSafe insights on current practices to understand how risks are being managed, to inform how it supports businesses to prevent harm.

WorkSafe’s visits to sheep, beef and dairy farms in 2025 found significant gaps in vehicle safety and hazardous substances management.

Following the 2025 assessments, WorkSafe developed free learning modules to help agricultural businesses and workers safely use and manage hazardous substances.

items.title: City Rail Link proves safety and scale can go hand in hand
items.summary: As Auckland celebrates the opening of the City Rail Link (CRL), WorkSafe New Zealand is recognising the project's high standard of health and safety performance, demonstrating what can be achieved when safety is embedded from the start.
items.readerText:
As Auckland celebrates the opening of the City Rail Link (CRL), WorkSafe New Zealand is recognising the project's high standard of health and safety performance, demonstrating what can be achieved when safety is embedded from the start.

The City Rail Link is the country’s largest transport infrastructure project and one of the country's most complex construction undertakings. With more than 21.5 million hours worked, the project recorded two incidents requiring hospital admission, setting a new benchmark for large-scale construction in New Zealand.

WorkSafe worked alongside CRL Limited and Link Alliance, the organisations responsible for overseeing and delivering the project, throughout its construction. The regulator provided expertise in underground construction, energy safety, occupational health, silica dust management and major project risk management.

WorkSafe’s Chief Inspector Extractives, Paul Hunt, says the project’s strong health and safety performance was driven by a high engagement approach that secured commitment at every level, from the boardroom through to the frontline workforce.

“It’s so important to get people on the same page with health and safety before the project even starts,” he says. “Most people want to get on board, as long as they understand it.”

“That’s what happened with City Rail Link – they were really open to it. We had regular meetings set up and on-the-ground inspectors met with on-the-ground project managers. It helped build trust and allow for collaboration to resolve any issues quickly.”

“This project demonstrates that serious harm is not inevitable in complex construction environments. Through strong leadership, effective risk management, and a commitment to continuous improvement, those involved in City Rail Link have shown what is possible.”

“The lessons from City Rail Link extend well beyond this project,” says Paul Hunt.

“The approaches developed here influenced major infrastructure projects elsewhere – such as the Christchurch Stadium and the recently opened Dunedin Hospital Outpatient building, which were also completed with outstanding safety results.”

“The real legacy of City Rail Link isn't just new transport infrastructure. It's demonstrating what can be achieved when everyone involved is committed to keeping people safe.”

items.title: Revised Achievement Standards and supporting materials for assessment in 2027 11/09/2026 Available now for planning purposes.
items.summary: Available now for planning purposes.
items.readerText:
A number of NCEA assessment materials have been updated for 2027 following the 2026 Review and Maintenance of NCEA. Teachers and other NCEA providers must ensure that all assessment in 2026 continues to use the current 2026 versions of Achievement Standards and supporting materials. A number of NCEA assessment materials have been updated for 2027 following the 2026 Review and Maintenance Programme. The Level 3 Te Ao Haka Achievement Standards, along with one Achievement Standard for Level 2 Economics (91227), have been updated during this process; the other updates have been made to assessment supporting materials. All updated NCEA materials for New Zealand Curriculum (NZC) are now available for 2027 planning purposes on the NCEA.Education website.

Draft External Assessment Specifications for 2027 will be available on the NZQA website.

NZC: The updates are available as PDFs, organised by subject, on the NCEA Support page. These are watermarked as “For Planning 2027”.

Te Marautanga o Aotearoa: Kaupae 2 and 3 Toi Puoro supporting materials and Tikanga Aromatawai for all subjects will be available on the NCEA Support page in Term 4.

The updated content is for use from 2027. In January 2027, the updated materials will replace the current materials on the NCEA.Education website for NZC Level 1 and Te Ao Haka Level 3; for NZC Levels 2 and 3, the materials will be updated on the TKI website. Once this has happened, the PDFs will be removed from NCEA.Education.

The Level 3 Te Ao Haka Achievement Standards and Level 2 Economics Achievement Standard (91227) that have been updated and are hosted on NZQA’s website will also be updated in January.

items.title: Driving safety success on major construction projects
items.summary: As Dunedin Hospital’s outpatient building opens, the project is also celebrating a major safety achievement: no serious injuries, supported by a new approach from WorkSafe New Zealand.
items.readerText:
As Dunedin Hospital’s outpatient building opens, the project is also celebrating a major safety achievement: no serious injuries, supported by a new approach from WorkSafe New Zealand.

Construction began in June 2022 and the building was officially opened last week, with the first patients expected through the doors in October.

WorkSafe inspectors used a new health and safety model, first developed by the regulator’s mining inspectors, to improve safety outcomes on the build.

Reducing harm in construction is a priority for WorkSafe. The sector accounts for around 15% of work-related fatalities and serious injuries and experiences some of the highest rates of acute and chronic harm.

Under the new model instead of sporadic site visits, inspectors worked closely with project teams through regular, consistent engagement. This approach has contributed to there being no major incidents on the build.

WorkSafe Dunedin area manager James Gourley introduced the model to the construction of the outpatient building after seeing its impact on the City Rail Link project in Auckland.

“It starts with early engagement at all levels, right from the boardroom to the frontline,” he says. “Traditionally, inspectors visit sites sporadically, often sending different personnel each time. This makes it hard to build rapport and address issues early.”

James Gourley and his team worked closely with contractor Southbase to embed monthly site visits by the same pair of inspectors. They also held regular senior leadership meetings with Health New Zealand, the project management and its health and safety advisors. The effect was noticeable.

“Toolbox safety talks are normally pretty quiet, but at the one I attended, the workers were speaking up,” he says. “They were passionate about it; the guys were really chiming in.”

Inspector Rob Bryson notes some compliance notices were issued at the start of the project, but that helped set expectations early.

“What came from it was an improvement in performance. In the later part of the build there were very few compliance notices; the issues became fewer. The construction teams knew the areas where they needed to perform better.”

Rob Bryson says trust was a defining outcome of the model.

“We’re showing we are reasonable; it’s not all about firing out enforcement notices. People understand what we’re trying to achieve, and they feel they can talk freely. If there was an issue, they’d call and let us know.”

Southbase’s Senior Project Manager Anthony Franicevic says the relationship-focused approach has helped dismantle a common misconception.

“There can be a perception on some sites that it’s us vs WorkSafe; that they’re hard to deal with, don’t call them. We worked hard together to shift that attitude and build trust. Having the same set of inspectors made all the difference.”

He says WorkSafe’s practical guidance, especially around dust and hazardous substances, has become part of everyday site culture.

“Normally we’d get a broom and sweep up the wood dust, but they asked, ‘Is there a better way to deal with that?’ So, we switched to vacuum systems. That’ll stay with me; it’s embedded in how I’ll operate in the future.”

The outpatient building is now complete and the next phase, the inpatient building, will be even larger, with up to 600 workers on site and completion scheduled for 2031.

But WorkSafe’s approach will stay the same.

Its Southern Region Manager Adrian van Dyk says the success of the model in Dunedin and Auckland will influence how the regulator works on major builds. “We have seen this approach being successful in the recently completed Te Kaha Stadium in Christchurch as well, which saw no major incidents across the full project.”

“I saw the good work James and his team put in on the Dunedin hospital project. They’ve created a model that works. It will lay the basis for how we develop our relationship with other contractors.”

We provide guidance, investigate serious incidents, and take enforcement action when necessary. We work with businesses, workers, and industry to reduce work-related harm and ensure everyone who goes to work comes home healthy and safe.

items.title: Food manufacturing visits finding safety gaps in machinery and hazardous substances
items.summary: WorkSafe inspectors have visited more than 300 food manufacturing businesses since July as part of our focus on the sector this quarter to support safer work.
items.readerText:
WorkSafe inspectors have visited more than 300 food manufacturing businesses since July as part of our focus on the sector this quarter to support safer work.

“At this midway point, the common issues requiring improvements are machinery safety and hazardous substances management,” says WorkSafe’s project lead Loren Molloy.

Machinery continues to be a main cause of harm in manufacturing, leading to about 200 injuries that result in more than a week off work each year.

Many serious injuries involve workers being caught in moving parts such as rollers, belts, or blades, often because machines were not adequately guarded or locked out.

A Christchurch commercial bakery was sentenced earlier this year after a worker’s hand was pulled into machine rollers, resulting in life-changing injuries.

Three critical safety failures that led to worker losing fingers

“WorkSafe expects businesses to identify their hazards and put effective controls in place,” says Loren Molloy. “For machinery, that means proper guarding, isolating machines before cleaning or maintenance, and making sure workers are trained to work safely.”

Hazardous substances recordkeeping and safe storage are also frequently being found to need improvement at assessment visits, with too many businesses not even having a hazardous substances inventory.

On a more positive note, inspectors have noted good worker engagement, participation and representation at many food manufacturing workplaces.

“It’s encouraging to see many food manufacturers actively involving their workers in health and safety, ensuring they can suggest improvements and raise concerns,” says Loren Molloy.

Our proactive food manufacturing assessments will continue until the end of September. This engagement with businesses and workers is key to WorkSafe helping them to meet their responsibilities to ensure work is healthy and safe.

Manufacturing has more injuries than any other sector, and food production is one of three manufacturing subsectors, alongside wood production and metal fabrication, where WorkSafe concentrates its effort.

Guidance to help manufacturing businesses manage their health and safety risks is available on our website

We will provide more detailed data and insights to show the overall picture from the assessments results later in the year.

A worker's life-changing injuries at a commercial bakery have exposed fundamental safety failures that WorkSafe says are far too common across New Zealand workplaces.

items.title: Unguarded farm machinery can change lives in seconds
items.summary: WorkSafe is reminding farmers to make sure all machinery guards are in place and regularly checked after a farm worker suffered life-changing injuries when he became entangled in an unguarded power take-off (PTO) shaft on a Wairarapa dairy farm.
items.readerText:
WorkSafe is reminding farmers to make sure all machinery guards are in place and regularly checked after a farm worker suffered life-changing injuries when he became entangled in an unguarded power take-off (PTO) shaft on a Wairarapa dairy farm.

The worker lost an arm and suffered multiple serious injuries after his clothing was caught in the unguarded PTO shaft while operating a tractor connected to a feed mixer in January 2025.

Shady Farming Limited pleaded guilty to a charge under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 and was convicted and fined an end total of $60,000 and ordered to pay reparation of approximately $96,000.

PTO shafts are one of the most hazardous parts of farm machinery. They rotate at high speed and when unguarded, can catch loose clothing in an instant, causing serious injuries or death.

WorkSafe’s Central Region Manager, Nigel Formosa, says the incident highlights why guarding machinery must be treated as a critical safety control.

“Farmers know PTOs are dangerous, yet we continue to see workers seriously injured by machinery that isn’t properly guarded.

“Guards are the last line of defence between a worker and a rotating shaft. If a guard is missing or damaged, the consequences can be devastating.”

The farm’s risk register recognised the high risk of entanglement with machinery and its safety management system required PTO shafts to always be guarded – no exceptions.

WorkSafe’s investigation found that the tractor and feed mixer were being operated without any guarding in place on the PTO shaft. Compliance with an adequate pre-start check and maintenance process was not effectively monitored. That process should have included checking guards were present and addressing any wear or damage by replacing damaged guards

“This incident shows that having rules on paper is not enough. Farmers need systems that ensure guards are actually present, in good condition, and checked before machinery is used,” says Nigel Formosa.

Regular inspections are particularly important because PTO guards can become damaged through normal farm operations and may need replacing.

check PTO shafts and other moving machinery parts are fully guarded

inspect guards regularly for wear, damage, or missing components

repair or replace damaged guards immediately

include guarding checks in documented pre-start inspections

ensure workers are trained to identify and report damaged or missing guards

keep well clear of PTO shafts and disengage machinery before approaching it.

Agriculture remains one of New Zealand’s highest-risk industries, and machinery-related incidents continue to cause serious harm.

“No job on the farm is so urgent that it justifies taking risks around moving machinery. A few minutes spent checking guards can prevent injuries that affect workers and their families for the rest of their lives,” says Nigel Formosa.

items.title: Check for asbestos before undertaking high-pressure spraying on roofs
items.summary: This safety alert is a reminder to consider whether asbestos-containing materials (ACM) may be present before carrying out high-pressure water spraying or using compressed air. Disturbing ACM can release asbestos fibres and contaminate surrounding areas, posing risks to workers, occupants, and others nearby.
items.readerText:
This safety alert is a reminder to consider whether asbestos-containing materials (ACM) may be present before carrying out high-pressure water spraying or using compressed air. Disturbing ACM can release asbestos fibres and contaminate surrounding areas, posing risks to workers, occupants, and others nearby.

WorkSafe has been notified of a number of instances in recent years where waterblasting was carried out on roofs which contained asbestos.

In the most recent case, the waterblasting work was carried out on a residential property built in the 1970s that had decramastic roof tiles.

Following the work, debris was identified across the property and inside the home. Testing later confirmed the roof tiles contained chrysotile asbestos and that asbestos-containing material had contaminated both indoor and outdoor areas.

Specialist assessment determined that remediation was required to address the contamination.

This incident highlights the importance of identifying whether asbestos-containing materials may be present before work begins, particularly when working on older buildings.

Decramastic roofing installed before asbestos was phased out may contain asbestos. Before undertaking work that could disturb roofing materials, asbestos risks should be identified and assessed.

Where asbestos-containing materials are known or suspected to be present, appropriate controls should be implemented before work starts. Controls should be selected based on the nature of the work and the risk of disturbing asbestos-containing material.

High-pressure water spraying (including water blasting) must not be used on asbestos or ACM. Likewise, compressed air must not be used on asbestos. Both are specifically prohibited under the Asbestos Regulations.

Thorough planning and assessment before work begins can help prevent asbestos exposure and reduce the risk of contamination to surrounding areas.

ACMs may be present before carrying out work on buildings built before the 2000s.

Identify and assess asbestos risks before undertaking waterblasting or other work that could disturb roofing materials.

Ensure appropriate controls are implemented where asbestos-containing materials are known or suspected to be present.

Where asbestos roofing is present, use an alternative method for cleaning that does not involve high pressure water or compressed air. For more information refer to Cleaning weathered asbestos containing roofing and cladding

If work has already started and asbestos-containing materials are identified or discovered, stop immediately and seek specialist advice.

Ensure workers understand asbestos risks and relevant safe work procedures.

More information about the safe handling of asbestos can be found at worksafe.govt.nz

High-pressure water blasting should not be used to clean roofing and cladding containing asbestos

items.title: WorkSafe releases practical guidance on workplace exposure standards
items.summary: WorkSafe New Zealand has released new plain-language resources to help businesses better understand workplace exposure standards (WES) and manage risks from harmful airborne substances.
items.readerText:
WorkSafe New Zealand has released new plain-language resources to help businesses better understand workplace exposure standards (WES) and manage risks from harmful airborne substances.

WES are guideline values that can help assess the risk of exposure to airborne substances such as dust and fumes. They are not compulsory limits or regulatory targets.

The new material includes educational videos, practical case studies, and a guide to working with occupational hygienists. WorkSafe has also updated inspector training and materials to support consistent frontline messaging.

The resources respond to feedback from industry stakeholders who said WES can be difficult to understand and apply, particularly where businesses face measurement costs, limited access to occupational hygienists, or uncertainty about what WorkSafe expects.

WorkSafe says the starting point for businesses is to eliminate or minimise exposure to harmful substances as far as reasonably practicable. WES can help assess exposure risk, but they are not compulsory limits, are not set in regulation, and are not designed for businesses to apply on their own.

“We heard clearly that businesses want practical guidance and confidence about what is expected of them,” says Kelly Hanson-White, DCE Insights and Engagement.

“Our focus is on helping businesses to understand their exposure risks and take action to manage them well, not looking at WES values as standalone enforcement thresholds.”

WorkSafe has also confirmed WES values for flour dust, softwood dust, hardwood dust, and welding fumes. Confirmed values are no longer interim, providing greater certainty for businesses and occupational hygiene and health specialists.

items.title: Changes to the health and safety law
items.summary: The Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (HSWA) sets out what businesses need to do to keep people healthy and safe at work. It also establishes key work health and safety principles and rights. Today, amendments to the Act received Royal Assent and became law with the changes coming into effect on 1 April 2027.
items.readerText:
As New Zealand’s primary work health and safety law, the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 (HSWA) sets out what businesses need to do to keep people healthy and safe at work. It also establishes key work health and safety principles and rights. Today, amendments to the Act received Royal Assent and became law with the changes coming into effect on 1 April 2027.

The amendments aim to focus the health and safety system on critical risk so that businesses are clear about the most important things to focus on. It’s part of the Government’s wider health and safety reforms.

From 1 April 2027, small businesses (those with fewer than 20 workers) will be required to manage critical risks and to prioritise critical risk when complying with other provisions of the Act and its regulations. Critical risks are those likely to cause the most serious harm. Larger businesses must manage all risks but prioritise those that are critical.

All businesses will need to identify critical risks based on what they should reasonably know about their work.

The ability for industry, worker, and employer organisations to develop their own codes of practice for approval by the Minister of Workplace Relations and Safety.

Providing clarity on the injuries and illnesses that must be notified to WorkSafe.

Prioritising certain functions for regulators like WorkSafe, such as providing guidance, developing and reviewing approved codes of practice (ACOPs), developing Safe Work Instruments, and monitoring and enforcing compliance.

Setting out that where a business follows an ACOP, it is taken to have complied with the Act meaning enforcement action cannot be taken about a relevant matter.

Narrower duties for landowners and officers.

Amending the WorkSafe Act to better support our focus on critical risks and educating businesses.

More information about the changes, and what they mean for businesses, will be available in the lead up to the Act’s commencement.

Understanding the changes to health and safety law

items.title: WorkSafe acknowledges the AUT study on asbestos-containing coloured sand
items.summary: WorkSafe acknowledges the independent research by Associate Professor Dr Terri-Ann Berry at Auckland University of Technology (AUT) into airborne asbestos fibres from affected coloured sand products.
items.readerText:
WorkSafe acknowledges the independent research by Associate Professor Dr Terri-Ann Berry at Auckland University of Technology (AUT) into airborne asbestos fibres from affected coloured sand products.

The results confirm that some of the recalled sand products can release respirable asbestos fibres into the air. We acknowledge that these findings may be concerning for those impacted, including workplaces and workers.

WorkSafe has completed an initial assessment of the study’s findings and, based on the information available, our advice for workplaces remains unchanged. WorkSafe’s advice has consistently been that any recalled or suspected affected coloured sand product in a workplace must be managed and removed as friable asbestos-containing material until proven otherwise.

Asbestos in coloured sand – advice for businesses

The findings reinforce the importance of taking a precautionary approach and support WorkSafe’s advice to date. However, the study at this time does not provide enough information to quantify the occupational exposure risk.

We will continue to monitor any emerging evidence and consider it in the context of workplace advice.

WorkSafe’s response to asbestos in coloured sand is based on the legal requirements set out in the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 and supporting regulations. We’re committed to supporting workplaces to manage their risks, ensuring they are well-informed about how to identify and manage any actual or potential presence of asbestos, and comply with the regulations.

Our inspectors have engaged with over 300 retailers and distribution centres. Our inspectors have observed a high-level of compliance and no enforcement action has been required.

WorkSafe is continuing to support the cross-agency response and to help ensure workplace health and safety advice is accurate, clear and consistent.

items.title: Food manufacturing in focus as proactive visits support safer work
items.summary: WorkSafe New Zealand is turning its attention to food product manufacturing, with a nationwide programme of proactive safety visits over the next three months.
items.readerText:
WorkSafe New Zealand is turning its attention to food product manufacturing, with a nationwide programme of proactive safety visits over the next three months.

Inspectors will carry out hundreds of planned visits to food manufacturers including bakeries, confectionery, grain, and cereal manufacturers to oil and fat, dairy, meat, seafood, and fruit and vegetable processors. Businesses will be contacted in advance to arrange a suitable time for an in-person visit, which typically takes about an hour.

“We want to help businesses understand their risks, and take practical steps to make work safer,” says WorkSafe's project lead, Loren Molloy. “Previous visits show this approach works – 73% of businesses visited by WorkSafe identified health and safety improvements because of their interaction with us.”

Manufacturing has more injuries than any other sector, and food product is one of three subsectors, alongside wood product and metal fabrication, where WorkSafe concentrates its effort.

“Machinery continues to be a leading cause of harm in manufacturing,” says Molloy. “Injuries from ineffective machine guarding and a lack of lockout/tagout practices come up repeatedly, particularly during cleaning, maintenance, or when workers are clearing jams.”

Many serious injuries involve workers being caught in moving parts such as rollers, belts, or blades, often because machines were not adequately guarded or locked out.

These risks aren’t hypothetical: a Christchurch commercial bakery was sentenced earlier this year after a worker’s hand was pulled into machine rollers, resulting in life-changing injuries.

“WorkSafe expects businesses to identify their hazards and put effective controls in place,” says Molloy. “For machinery, that means proper guarding, isolating machines before cleaning or maintenance, and making sure workers are trained to work safely.”

Other common issues found in past assessments included poor hazardous substances recordkeeping and storage, inadequate dust and fume controls, and incorrect PPE (personal protective equipment) use.

Workplace culture makes a real difference. Strong leadership, clear expectations, and worker involvement support good practice and ensures concerns are raised, while a “just get the job done” mindset can let unsafe habits become normal.

“We sometimes hear the attitude that ‘it's just a two-minute job’, but even a quick routine task can cause life-changing injuries or death if it’s not done safely,” says Molloy.

Insights about the assessment findings will be shared publicly later in the year.

items.title: WorkSafe helps hundreds of wood manufacturers lift their safety game
items.summary: WorkSafe New Zealand has provided practical safety guidance to hundreds of wood manufacturing businesses, as part of a significant proactive focus on one of the country's most dangerous sectors.
items.readerText:
WorkSafe New Zealand has provided practical safety guidance to hundreds of wood manufacturing businesses, as part of a significant proactive focus on one of the country's most dangerous sectors.

WorkSafe’s health and safety inspectors visited 657 businesses between January and March – from toy makers to joiners and wood processors – sharing education and guidance material with 83% of them.

“Many businesses were committed to improving safety and welcomed the chance to talk through their health and safety practices,” says WorkSafe’s project lead Savio Valladares. “These visits are about helping businesses get it right, not catching them out.”

However, the assessments also revealed persistent safety gaps. About half the businesses visited were required to make prompt changes to help prevent harm. The most common issues were inadequate machine guarding, missing or out-of-date hazardous substances inventories, and workers exposed to wood dust without effective controls such as ventilation and protective equipment.

“Manufacturing workers deserve to go home healthy and safe at the end of every day. These visits are about helping businesses and workers understand what good looks like – and most were receptive to that. While we can see progress is being made, too many are still missing safety essentials,” says Savio Valladares.

The findings reinforce why the sector is a priority focus for WorkSafe. Manufacturing has the highest rate and number of injuries resulting in more than a week off work of any sector – around 200 machinery-related injuries occur each year. An average of four to five manufacturing workers are killed at work each year – roughly two thirds of fatalities occur in food, wood, and metal product manufacturing.

WorkSafe will continue proactive visits to manufacturing businesses. From July to September, the focus shifts to food manufacturing.

WorkSafe’s role is to influence businesses and workers to meet their responsibilities and keep people healthy and safe.

On 1 October 2026, the New Zealand School Property Agency (NZSPA) will be established as a Crown entity, to manage, plan, build, maintain and administer the education property portfolio. Our School Property team is transferring to NZSPA so schools and stakeholders can continue to work with them or their local property advisor for support. Establishing NZSPA

The latest curriculum, assessment, and aromatawai news for schools and kura.

As May draws to a close, we acknowledge the significant progress across kura and schools as updated curriculum, assessment, and teaching supports move into everyday practice.

This update brings together recent announcements, newly available resources, and key updates to support your planning and practice.

Below you’ll find key highlights and links to Tāhūrangi to help you focus on what matters most for ākonga.

Ngā mihi nui Te Tāhuhu o te Mātauranga | Ministry of Education

The Government has announced a range of investments through Budget 2026 to support teaching and learning across Aotearoa New Zealand. These include funding to strengthen curriculum delivery, assessment, and supports for kaiako and ākonga.

Further detail on the education package and what it means for schools and kura is available on our website.

Pre-Budget commitment for Curriculum and Assessment #

As part of Budget 2026, the Government has pre-committed over $131 million to further support Literacy and Te Reo Matatini, Maths and Pāngarau for Years 0 to 10. This includes the implementation of a Foundational Learning Action Plan.

More information about the funding package and Action Plan is available on our website.

Updated implementation timeframe for Years 0–8 curriculum #

The implementation timeline for the refreshed Years 0–8 national curriculum has been extended to give principals and tumuaki more time to lead change in schools and kura.

From the start of 2027, schools are expected to begin using the new Science, Social Sciences, Pūtaiao, and Pūmanawa Tangata learning areas, with full implementation phased across 2027 and 2028.

The remaining Years 0–8 curriculum will be implemented from 2029.

All Years 9–10 content for both the New Zealand Curriculum and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa must still be taught from the start of 2027.

New timeframe for Years 0-8 final National Curriculum – Tāhūrangi

Further details on new senior secondary qualifications #

The Government recently released further details about the new qualifications that will replace NCEA from 2028.

These subject-based qualifications are designed to be clearer, credible, and internationally comparable, and will align with the refreshed, knowledge-rich senior secondary curriculum currently being finalised.

New Zealand Certificate of Education (NZCE) will be introduced for Year 12.

New Zealand Advanced Certificate of Education (NZACE) will be introduced for Year 13.

A new Foundational Award, focused on literacy and numeracy at a Year 11 benchmark, will also be available.

New senior secondary qualifications replacing NCEA – Tāhūrangi

Consultation open on first group of Years 11–13 subjects #

Consultation opened this month on the first group of 26 subjects for the new Years 11–13 curriculum, with feedback open until 15 June.

The subjects have been developed with input from more than 300 teachers and education leaders across Aotearoa New Zealand, alongside Subject Associations.

Consultation open on first group of Years | Tau 11–13 curriculum subjects – Tāhūrangi

Pūmanawa Tangata released – Last TMoA wāhanga ako #

The last draft Years 0 to 10 wāhanga ako in Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is available for consultation until 5 June.

Pūmanawa Tangata replaces Tikanga ā Iwi in Te Marautanga o Aotearoa and was previously known as Te Ao Māori.

This wāhanga ako will prepare mokopuna for learning in History, Geography, Social Studies, Classical Studies, Education for Sustainability, Economics, Business Studies, and wider social science and civic focused learning.

Draft Years 0–10 Pūmanawa Tangata released for consultation – Tāhūrangi

Available now: New curriculum resources released #

We're continuing to release new teaching resources to help you to start planning and teaching the draft and updated curricula.

Bookmark these webpages so you know what’s available and what’s coming.

Teaching resources to support the updated New Zealand Curriculum – Tāhūrangi

Teaching resources to support the updated Te Marautanga o Aotearoa – Tāhūrangi

Supports available now to implement Te Marautanga o Aotearoa #

A range of supports are available, and more are coming, to help kaiako and kura confidently implement the refreshed curriculum.

Practical classroom examples, including teaching guidance, unit plans and activities (Pāngarau kit arriving this term, others follow in Term 3).

Wāhanga ako learning kits (Tau 9–10) – Tāhūrangi

Wāhanga ako banners and professional learning activities to support shared understanding and sense‑making (Pāngarau and Te Reo Rangatira) are available, others follow in Term 3 with the release of the finalised curriculum.

Curriculum overview products – Tāhurangi

Existing Te Marautanga o Aotearoa resources

Available now to support planning and implementation.

Existing Te Marautanga o Aotearoa resources – Tāhūrangi

Available now: Reo Māori lessons (Term 3 EOIs open) #

Expressions of interest are open for Term 3 Ministry-funded online reo Māori lessons for kaiako and kaimahi (Years 0–13).

Te Kura Raunui offers beginner (Rautahi) and foundational (Raurua) reo Māori lessons.

Te Rākau Taumatua provides advanced reo Māori lessons for more proficient speakers.

Participants can use a self-assessment tool to find the right level and do not need to complete earlier levels before applying.

Find out more and submit an expression of interest – Tāhūrangi

For leaders: Curriculum leadership PLD (self-directed) #

School or kura leaders can access new PLD resources (self-directed) to support implementation of curriculum changes from 6 May.

Curriculum Leadership PLD resources for English medium – Tāhūrangi

Curriculum Leadership PLD resources for Māori medium – Tāhūrangi

Apply now: Online writing acceleration tool for Years 6 to 10 #

More than 450 schools have registered to use Scribo, the online writing acceleration tool. This accelerated support is for students from Years 6 to 10 who are not yet meeting curriculum expectations in writing.

You can still apply to be part of the programme via Salesforce, providing an indication of the numbers of students and teachers likely to access the tool. Applications for cohort 2 close 5 June.

Writing acceleration supports – Tāhūrangi

For your planning: New parent and whānau reporting statement #

A new statement is now available to support schools in introducing updated reporting approaches to parents and whānau.

The statement explains that schools will begin using the new reporting components during 2026, with full changes becoming more visible over time.

Reporting to parents and whānau – Tāhūrangi

The first SMART reporting window has now closed. Thank you to schools and kura who completed assessments and submissions during this period.

For the 2026 school year, schools can choose between SMART, e-asTTle or PAT for twice-yearly progression monitoring. The second SMART reporting window opens in Term 4, running from 12 October to 13 November.

You can continue to access marking guidance, exemplars, rubrics, and reporting support on Tāhūrangi.

Latest Curriculum Insights study results released #

The 2025 Curriculum Insights report is available, giving the strongest national picture yet of how students in English-medium settings are progressing in reading, writing, and mathematics.

The 2025 results show that student achievement has largely stabilised, with early upward shifts in maths and writing.

These early signs are encouraging, particularly given that most curriculum, assessment and professional learning supports have been in place for less than 4 school terms.

Student achievement stable during curriculum rollout, with small improvements in some areas - Curriculum Insights

NZCER releases interim mapping from PATs to progress descriptors #

NZCER has published interim mapping from PAT Pāngarau | Mathematics and PAT Pānui | Reading Comprehension to the progress descriptors, for reporting against the refreshed New Zealand Curriculum.

These tables build on interim mapping work for e-asTTle conducted by the Ministry and will be updated later in the year to reflect curriculum alignment work being undertaken for the SMART tool. NZCER will also be releasing similar mapping for PAT Tuhituhi | Writing.

Read more about the mapping, the methodology behind it and how to use this information in your reporting at the NZCER website.

Interim mapping of PAT results to Progress Descriptors now available – NZCER

Updated implementation timeframe for Years 0–8 curriculum#

The implementation timeline for the refreshed Years 0–8 national curriculum has been extended to give principals and tumuaki more time to lead change in schools and kura.

From the start of 2027, schools are expected to begin using the new Science, Social Sciences, Pūtaiao, and Pūmanawa Tangata learning areas, with full implementation phased across 2027 and 2028.

The remaining Years 0–8 curriculum will be implemented from 2029.

All Years 9–10 content for both the New Zealand Curriculum and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa must still be taught from the start of 2027.

New timeframe for Years 0-8 final National Curriculum – Tāhūrangi

Further details on new senior secondary qualifications#

The Government recently released further details about the new qualifications that will replace NCEA from 2028.

These subject-based qualifications are designed to be clearer, credible, and internationally comparable, and will align with the refreshed, knowledge-rich senior secondary curriculum currently being finalised.

From 2028:

  • New Zealand Certificate of Education (NZCE) will be introduced for Year 12.
  • New Zealand Advanced Certificate of Education (NZACE) will be introduced for Year 13.
  • A new Foundational Award, focused on literacy and numeracy at a Year 11 benchmark, will also be available.

New senior secondary qualifications replacing NCEA – Tāhūrangi

Have your say#

Consultation open on first group of Years 11–13 subjects#

Consultation opened this month on the first group of 26 subjects for the new Years 11–13 curriculum, with feedback open until 15 June.

The subjects have been developed with input from more than 300 teachers and education leaders across Aotearoa New Zealand, alongside Subject Associations.

Consultation open on first group of Years | Tau 11–13 curriculum subjects – Tāhūrangi

Pūmanawa Tangata released – Last TMoA wāhanga ako#

The last draft Years 0 to 10 wāhanga ako in Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is available for consultation until 5 June.

Pūmanawa Tangata replaces Tikanga ā Iwi in Te Marautanga o Aotearoa and was previously known as Te Ao Māori.

This wāhanga ako will prepare mokopuna for learning in History, Geography, Social Studies, Classical Studies, Education for Sustainability, Economics, Business Studies, and wider social science and civic focused learning.

Draft Years 0–10 Pūmanawa Tangata released for consultation – Tāhūrangi

Supports and resources#

Available now: New curriculum resources released#

We're continuing to release new teaching resources to help you to start planning and teaching the draft and updated curricula.

Bookmark these webpages so you know what’s available and what’s coming.

Teaching resources to support the updated New Zealand Curriculum – Tāhūrangi

Teaching resources to support the updated Te Marautanga o Aotearoa – Tāhūrangi

Supports available now to implement Te Marautanga o Aotearoa#

A range of supports are available, and more are coming, to help kaiako and kura confidently implement the refreshed curriculum.

Wāhanga ako learning kits (Tau 9–10)

Practical classroom examples, including teaching guidance, unit plans and activities (Pāngarau kit arriving this term, others follow in Term 3).

Wāhanga ako learning kits (Tau 9–10) – Tāhūrangi

Wāhanga ako banners and professional learning activities to support shared understanding and sense‑making (Pāngarau and Te Reo Rangatira) are available, others follow in Term 3 with the release of the finalised curriculum.

Existing Te Marautanga o Aotearoa resources

Available now to support planning and implementation.

Existing Te Marautanga o Aotearoa resources – Tāhūrangi

Expressions of interest are open for Term 3 Ministry-funded online reo Māori lessons for kaiako and kaimahi (Years 0–13).

  • Te Kura Raunui offers beginner (Rautahi) and foundational (Raurua) reo Māori lessons.
  • Te Rākau Taumatua provides advanced reo Māori lessons for more proficient speakers.

Participants can use a self-assessment tool to find the right level and do not need to complete earlier levels before applying.

Find out more and submit an expression of interest – Tāhūrangi

School or kura leaders can access new PLD resources (self-directed) to support implementation of curriculum changes from 6 May.

Curriculum Leadership PLD resources for English medium – Tāhūrangi

Curriculum Leadership PLD resources for Māori medium – Tāhūrangi

More than 450 schools have registered to use Scribo, the online writing acceleration tool. This accelerated support is for students from Years 6 to 10 who are not yet meeting curriculum expectations in writing.

You can still apply to be part of the programme via Salesforce, providing an indication of the numbers of students and teachers likely to access the tool. Applications for cohort 2 close 5 June.

Writing acceleration supports – Tāhūrangi

Assessment, reporting and insights#

For your planning: New parent and whānau reporting statement#

A new statement is now available to support schools in introducing updated reporting approaches to parents and whānau.

The statement explains that schools will begin using the new reporting components during 2026, with full changes becoming more visible over time.

The first SMART reporting window has now closed. Thank you to schools and kura who completed assessments and submissions during this period.

The 2025 Curriculum Insights report is available, giving the strongest national picture yet of how students in English-medium settings are progressing in reading, writing, and mathematics.

The 2025 results show that student achievement has largely stabilised, with early upward shifts in maths and writing.

items.title: NCEA update: structure of new qualification system agreed 26/03/2026 Information regarding an update to NCEA and structure of a new qualification system.
items.summary: Information regarding an update to NCEA and structure of a new qualification system.
items.readerText:
The Government has agreed to the structure of a new qualification system to replace the National Certificate of Educational Achievement (NCEA).

The announcement by the Minister of Education, the Hon Erica Stanford, on 26 March is available here and follows a consultation process with more than 10,000 having their say.

Today’s announcement is the first major milestone in a carefully sequenced set of decisions to design a modern qualification system that will align with the new knowledge rich curriculum.

Cabinet approved an initial package outlining the structural components of the new qualification system. These include:

Replacing NCEA with a new secondary qualifications system with two levels over two years at Years 12 & 13.

Introducing subject-based assessment for Years 12 & 13, ensuring students are assessed on whole curriculum subjects.

Removing NCEA Level 1 and replacing it with deeper, curriculum-driven learning in Year 11. This will better prepare students for the qualification in Years 12 and 13.

Introducing a Foundational Award recognising students’ achievement in literacy and numeracy at a Year 11 curriculum level.

A requirement that all Year 11 students study English | Te Reo Rangatira and Mathematics | Pāngarau from 2028.

Integrating industry-led subjects into the senior curriculum, providing a single qualification pathway.

This is the first tranche in the design of the new qualification system. The detailed design of the new qualification will now get underway and the Ministry will be undertaking targeted engagement and working with the new Technical Advisory Group. Tranche two includes achievement requirements for Year 12 and 13; whether the Foundational Award is a requirement for the Year 12 and 13 qualifications; and more information about how grading is going to work, for example what scale is used for grading. Assessment will be developed to incentivise learning and achievement, better preparing students for life after school.

Find out more information on Tāhūrangi.education.govt.nz https://tahurangi.education.govt.nz/ncea_tranche1

items.title: Reviewed NZC & TMoA Achievement Standards and assessment materials published for 2026 21/01/2026 On each subject page, use the Recent Changes button to see a summary of updates.
items.summary: On each subject page, use the Recent Changes button to see a summary of updates.
items.readerText:
A number of standards and supporting materials have been updated for 2026. These updates are a result of the annual NCEA review and maintenance programme (RAMP). This year’s RAMP updates affect a number of New Zealand Curriculum (NZC) and Te Marautanga o Aotearoa (TMoA) subjects across NCEA Levels 1, 2, and 3.

Teachers and other NCEA providers must ensure that the revised standards and supporting materials are used for assessment in 2026.

There are no changes to the competencies being assessed by the Achievement Standards. Most of the updates are very minor and have been made to improve clarity and interpretation. It is important to note that the Conditions of Assessment have been updated for all internal assessments | aromatawai ā-roto to provide clearer guidance around authenticity.

All affected Achievement Standards and supporting materials were made available as PDFs for planning purposes on the NCEA website in September 2025. These PDFs have now been removed and materials on the relevant subject pages have been updated for use in 2026. For externally assessed | aromatawai ā-waho Achievement Standards with changes to the method of assessment, External Assessment Specifications | Tautuhinga Aromatawai for 2026 are available on the NZQA website, here: 2026 NCEA and NZ Scholarship assessment specifications - NZQA

Where to find updated Standards and materials

Level 1 NZC and TMoA subjects: 2026 updates are available on the relevant subject pages on the NCEA website. A summary of changes made is available in the Recent Changes section of each subject page and achievement standard.

All Level 1 Conditions of Assessment for internal achievement standards are available in the Assessment | Te Aromatawai tab of each subject page.

Subjects with other RAMP updates include: English, New Zealand Sign Language, Health Studies, Physical Education, Dance, Drama, Music, Te Ao Haka, Visual Arts, Te Reo Māori, Gagana Sāmoa, Gagana Tokelau, Lea Faka-Tonga, Te Reo Māori Kūki Āirani, Vagahau Niue, French, German, Spanish, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Mathematics and Statistics, Design and Visual Communications, Digital Technologies, Materials and Processing Technology, Chemistry and Biology, Physics, Earth and Space Science, Science, Commerce, Geography, Social Studies, Te Reo Rangatira, Hauora and Pāngarau.

Levels 2 and 3 NZC subjects: 2026 updates are available on the relevant subject pages of the TKI website: Resources for internally assessed achievement standards / NCEA on TKI - NCEA. All Level 2 and 3 Conditions of Assessment for internal achievement standards are available in each subject page.

Subjects with other RAMP updates include: English, Health, Chinese, Cook Islands, French, German, Japanese, Korean, Lea-Faka Tonga, NZ Sign Language, Samoan, Te Reo Māori, Te Ao Haka, Agricultural and Horticultural Science, Biology, Earth and Space Science, Economics, History, Psychology, Social Studies, Digital Technologies, Design and Visual Communication.

Level 2 and 3 TMoA: Existing materials and resources are now available for kaiako on the NCEA website . These include: Te Reo Rangatira, Ngā Mahi a te Rēhia, Toi Ataata, Toi Puoro, Tikanga ā-Iwi, Hangarau, Hauora, Pāngarau, and Pūtaiao.

Level 1-3 Te Ao Haka: 2026 updates are available on the relevant Te Ao Haka subject pages on the NCEA website . Video resources will be available on the website in Term 2 to support the Te Ao Haka changes. A summary of changes made is available in the Recent Changes section of the Te Ao Haka subject page and each TAH achievement standard.

Te Reo Matatini and Pāngarau Unit Standards have been updated for clarity and the NCEA website has been updated with links to the latest versions.

All PDFs for planning purposes have now been removed from the NCEA.Ed website.

If you have any questions, please contact the NCEA team at NCEA.Review@education.govt.nz

Kua whakaputaina ngā whakahounga o ngā Paerewa Paetae me ngā rauemi aromatawai mō te NZC me TMoA

Assessment specifications provide the annual assessment parameters for each externally assessed achievement standard and New Zealand Scholarship performance standard. They must be read alongside the applicable standards.

The assessment specifications for subjects externally assessed by examinations include the:

context for questions, where appropriate.

For the submitted portfolios or reports, they include the:

portfolio/report specifications, including the type and volume of materials that may be submitted as evidence.

Some 2026 assessment specifications have recently been updated to provide further clarification of the requirements and conditions of the assessment.

The following Scholarship subjects have amended assessment specifications to reflect the option of a candidate being able take the examination digitally:

The following subjects have had a change of submission date:

Technology, Level 2 and Level 3 changed to 28 October 2026

Visual Arts, Level 3 and Scholarship changed to 2 November 2026

Other assessment specifications have amendments, as follows:

Design and Visual Communication, Level 1, 92002, 92003

Design and Visual Communication, Level 2, 91337, 91338, 91339

Design and Visual Communication, Level 3, 91627

Digital Technologies, Scholarship, 93604

New Zealand Sign Language, Level 1, 92357, 92358

Technology, Level 2, 91358, 91359, 91360, 91363

Technology, Level 3, 91612, 91613, 91614, 91617

Visual Arts, Level 2, 91320, 91321, 91322, 91323, 91324

Visual Arts, Level 3, 91455, 91456, 91457, 91458, 91459

Visual Arts, Scholarship, 93306, 93307, 93308, 93309, 93310

Visual Arts Sculpture (Level 3 and NZ Scholarship)

In 2025, NZQA conducted a live trial with Level 3 and NZ Scholarship Sculpture to determine the feasibility of submitting digitally and assessing the material digitally. The trial was a valuable learning experience for NZQA and in that respect we can consider the trial a success. The trial uncovered a range of nuanced complexities that will need to be carefully worked through before a digital submission is re-introduced.

The 2026 submission process for Level 3 and Scholarship Sculpture will, therefore, revert back to the physical portfolio submission process used up to 2024. The assessment method has now been updated in the assessment specifications.

2026 Tautuhinga Aromatawai (Assessment Specifications)

Final versions of the 2026 Tautuhinga Aromatawai for the following subjects/wāhanga ako were published on 9 February.

There are no further updates to these. The final versions can be found on the subject pages.

Special Assessment Conditions (SAC) Notification Gateway

NZQA has completed a review of SAC processes and has introduced several changes from 2026, including an expansion of the Notifications Gateway. The updated system will simplify SAC applications while ensuring decisions remain evidence-based and aligned with the needs of students/ākonga.

When making new SAC applications for students/ākonga undertaking assessment of standards listed in the Directory of Assessment and Skill Standards, schools can choose either the Approvals Gateway to submit applications for NZQA approval, or the Notifications Gateway to inform NZQA of student/ākonga needs and the SAC required.

Outcomes of the 2025 biennial consultation on the New Zealand Scholarship subject list (the List)

Every two years, NZQA consults with the education sector and other interested groups about the subjects assessed in New Zealand Scholarship.

NZQA sought feedback between 12 June and 11 July 2025 on subjects to be included on, or excluded from, the List from 2027. Feedback was not sought on any specific subject. Respondents could free-type the subjects they wanted to provide feedback on, rather than selecting from a pre-populated list.

Go to the current Scholarship subject list

The biennial review aims to maintain the credibility of Scholarship by ensuring subjects:

are relevant and meet government and sector expectations

can be administered effectively and efficiently, and

have sufficient workforce supply to support quality assessment at the appropriate level.

How New Zealand Scholarship subjects are selected

three supported splitting Health and Physical into two separate subjects.

Agribusiness, Business Studies and Social Studies had 11, 15 and 1 submission respectively in support of their inclusion.

All feedback was considered, and each subject was assessed against the criteria for inclusion. The inclusion of Lea Faka Tonga was also reconsidered.

The following outcomes were endorsed by NZQA’s Technical Overview Group Assessment and agreed by the NZQA Board:

Health and Physical Education to remain as a single subject.

Agribusiness is not added to the list at this time.

Business Studies is added to the list from 2027.

Social Studies is not added to the list at this time.

Lea Faka Tonga is not added to the list at this time.

The next review is planned for 2027, to determine subjects for inclusion or exclusion from 2029.

Note: 2025 is the final year that Scholarship Latin will be offered.

items.title: 2027 Examination timetable date range A2026/3
items.summary: This circular contains information about the 2027 examination timetable date range
items.readerText:
The 2027 End of Year Examination Timetable for NCEA and New Zealand Scholarship will run from Tuesday 9 November until Friday 3 December 2027. No sessions will be scheduled for Canterbury Anniversary Day (observed Friday 12 November 2027) and the Chatham Islands and Westland Anniversary days (observed on Monday 29 November 2027).

This date range is the same length as for the 2026 NCEA and New Zealand Scholarship end of year examinations.

Please refer any enquiries relating to this circular to your School Relationship Manager.

items.title: 2026 Examination Timetable dates and intra-year Assessment Timetable - A2025/12
items.summary: The published end-of-year examination dates for 2026 have been pushed back a week to allow more time for teaching and learning in Term 4, and to enable students to be better prepared for external assessments.
items.readerText:
The published end-of-year examination dates for 2026 have been pushed back a week to allow more time for teaching and learning in Term 4, and to enable students to be better prepared for external assessments.

The 2026 End of Year Examination Timetable for NCEA and New Zealand Scholarship will run from Tuesday 10 November until Friday 4 December 2026. No sessions are scheduled for the following regional anniversary days:

Canterbury Anniversary Day (observed Friday 13 November 2026)

Westland Anniversary Day and Chatham Islands Anniversary Day (observed Monday 30 November 2026).

Te Ao Haka TAPā external assessments have been moved into the end-of-year examination period to allow more time for teaching and learning, and to enable students to be better prepared for the external assessments.

TAPā with dates yet to be confirmed will be published as soon as is practicable.

The full 2026 examination timetable will be published in early December 2025, following the conclusion of the 2025 examinations.

The previously published 2026 intra-year assessment dates for Literacy and Numeracy and Te Reo Matatini me te Pāngarau have been changed to avoid clashing with significant events.

Please refer any enquiries relating to this circular to your School Relationship Manager.
